name: Colin Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. Walk me through a normal shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and a junior agent on evening calls and chats at the contact centre. I finished secondary school and still ask a skilled agent to check the difficult bills. The evening rate makes this job pay better than many call jobs, and I like helping someone sort a charge before going home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What waits at home when the shift ends?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife works in a school kitchen. We have a mortgage, children aged eight and eleven, and about eight months of expenses saved after a roof repair. Several other centres are nearby, but I won't lose this evening premium just to get a different title. I use AI search now and then after someone has shown me it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the late shift the little search tool saves us looking through old chats. I would still check the account before promising a refund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly secure. I'm a junior who still asks for help on complicated bills, but the evening rate pays well and my wife and I have eight months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my evening calls and use the approved search tool only for cases another agent has already checked. Through the first year I'll replace the savings we spent on a roof repair before buying anything for the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about work, with the usual unease when a hard caller waits. Our mortgage is manageable while both wages hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who shares the household bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife works in a school kitchen, and the children are eight and eleven. We built the reserve slowly because a roof repair and a school bill can arrive together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What has the search tool got wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I once found an old answer that used the wrong fee. Now I compare the source record before I repeat anything to a caller.

say: I'd say **search tools** speed up finding old chats.
I'd still check the **source account** before any refund promise.
think: I feel **secure** with high evening pay and eight months saved.
I know my **junior skill gap** still shows on complex bills.
do: Keep taking **evening calls** during the first year.
Use the **approved search tool** only on checked case types.
Rebuild our **eight-month reserve** after the roof repair.
feel: **Calm** about work, with ordinary nerves on hard calls.
S0.quote: We built the reserve slowly because a roof repair and a school bill can arrive together.
fieldNote: His **evening rate** explains high pay despite junior standing.
He uses **AI occasionally** only after another agent proves the case type.
The **roof repair** made the household reserve concrete.

steps.text: Keep answering customer calls on the evening shift
Rebuild eight months of household savings after roof repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should count the calls that come back after the machine answers. A faster first reply is no gain if I have to untangle the bill twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the easy evening chats that teach me the job could disappear. Eight months saved and several centres nearby give us time, but I might lose the premium that makes this wage good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare twenty closed billing chats with the new checker beside an experienced agent. If my evening hours fall in the first year, I'll apply for posted paid shifts at another centre only if the offered wage and hours cover our mortgage and replace the lost premium.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the evening roster, though I can afford a short search. I would rather see the numbers than guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count in the test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mark each repeat call and ask whether the original answer caused it. I would take the results to the team meeting with the agent who checked them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a new shift need to pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I won't leave for a day-shift title if it cuts our monthly income. I need the full written schedule and rate before I give notice.

say: I'd count **repeat calls** after automated answers.
I'd compare **wrong bills** as well as speed before judging the tool.
think: I may lose **easy evening chats** before I master harder bills.
I fear losing the **shift premium** even with a strong reserve.
do: Test **twenty closed chats** with a senior agent this month.
Bring **repeat-call results** to the next team meeting together.
Apply for **posted shifts** after cuts only at mortgage-covering total pay replacing the premium; leave only after written terms.
feel: **Anxious** about the roster, with savings for a short search.
S1.quote: I won't leave for a day-shift title if it cuts our monthly income.
fieldNote: His **premium pay** is at risk even if a new role sounds similar.
He wants **joint evidence** from a senior agent before taking a claim to management.
His **eight-month reserve** buys search time but not a replacement wage.

steps.text: Test twenty closed billing chats with the new checker and senior agent
Apply for posted paid shifts after cuts only if wages and hours cover mortgage and premium
Keep current evening wage until written schedule and rate replace the premium and cover mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 could answer our billing calls before the centre has another use for juniors. Robots around 2031 do not postpone what happens to a headset.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my calls could go, and other nearby centres might make the same cut. Our eight-month reserve would cover a search, but my wife's kitchen wage cannot carry the mortgage and two children by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll collect my pay records and ask for written notice dates. If my post ends in the first year after 2028, I'll apply for posted paid inventory jobs at local shops, checking wages and hours against the mortgage; I won't pay for a certificate until a posted job requires it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and awake at night. Eight months is real money, but it runs down when an entire field changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your wife?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my wife the evening premium may vanish and show her the figures from our budget. We would cut the planned furniture purchase before touching the mortgage reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would inventory work be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop work is hands-on for now, though robots could reach it around 2031. I'd ask the manager what people still do before I spend money learning stock systems.

say: I'd warn that **2028 AGI** could remove junior billing calls.
I'd explain **2031 robots** offer our headsets no extra time.
think: I expect my **call job** could end along with nearby centre openings.
I know **eight months saved** cannot replace my wage indefinitely.
do: Request **written notice dates** and keep pay records now.
Apply for **posted paid inventory work** after a cut only if wages and hours cover mortgage.
Delay the **furniture purchase** if my premium income stops.
feel: **Anxious** about a broad cut despite an eight-month reserve.
S2.quote: Eight months is real money, but it runs down when an entire field changes.
fieldNote: He sees **inventory work** as a short bridge before hands-on robots.
He protects the **mortgage reserve** by delaying furniture first.
He requires a **posted job** before spending on a certificate.

steps.text: Apply for posted paid inventory work after a cut only if wages and hours cover mortgage
Delay buying new furniture if the evening premium stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues five years gives us a chance to learn the harder cases while the centre still pays us. Our billing work faces thinking AI in 2031, before hands-on robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could become quicker on disputes by then, but even that work may be automated. I would use the time to check real paid stock jobs, not assume my evening rate lasts forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep the late shift and ask to sit with a skilled agent on one dispute each week. If a local shop advertises paid inventory work with enough hours and wages for our mortgage, I'll take a paid trial; in the first year after 2031 I'll apply only for a posted role whose offer covers the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but the calendar gives me room to test. I can keep earning while I decide whether the physical work suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a stockroom trial show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to see a full delivery morning, not just a quiet afternoon in the stockroom. I'd ask whether workers still handle those tasks as robots approach 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you study before an offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn't quit for a course. I'd practise on my current paid calls and pay for training only when a posted job requires it and the fee fits outside our mortgage reserve.

say: I'd use **five years** to learn difficult calls while paid.
I'd tell coworkers **2034 robots** come after our 2031 call risk.
think: I could become **quicker on disputes** before 2031.
I doubt better **call skill** alone protects my evening wage from AGI.
do: Keep my **paid late shift** while it remains open.
Practise **one disputed call** weekly with a skilled agent.
Try **paid inventory work** only with a posted opening whose wages and hours cover mortgage.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to test work while earning.
S3.quote: I want to see a full delivery morning, not just a quiet afternoon in the stockroom.
fieldNote: He needs to test a **full shift** before treating stock work as income.
His **current call practice** is part of staying employed, not a speculative course.
He checks the **2034 robot date** before buying stockroom training.

steps.text: Keep taking paid evening calls and practising weekly disputes
Try posted paid inventory work only if offered wages and hours cover mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets families compare real jobs while the centre still has staff to teach juniors. Thinking AI reaches our calls in 2036; robots arrive for hands-on work around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 the children may be older, but our mortgage could remain. I would not plan on a shop job being safe forever, or on every contact centre surviving unchanged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep the late shift and add part of the premium to savings each month. I'll check posted shop and centre vacancies twice yearly; after AGI arrives in 2036, I'll move only if my call hours fall and a written paid offer covers our mortgage and has steady hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about the long runway. I can make one careful decision at a time while the pay is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to reach a full year of household expenses saved, but only by adding from paid shifts. If the premium disappears, we revise the target instead of pretending we saved money we did not earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn how to check a bill and how to ask what a job actually pays. A prediction is not a wage slip.

say: I'd compare **real paid jobs** across the decade, including their hours and take-home wages before changing fields.
I'd distinguish **2036 calls** from hands-on robots around 2039.
think: I may still owe on the **mortgage** at 53.
I cannot assume **stock or call work** will stay safe unchanged.
do: Keep my **late shift** while it pays well.
Save part of the **evening premium** toward one year of expenses.
Move after 2036 only if **hours fall** and a written paid offer has steady hours and wages covering the mortgage.
feel: **Mostly calm** with time and a current good wage.
S4.quote: A prediction is not a wage slip.
fieldNote: His **savings target** depends on a continuing shift premium.
He checks **shop and centre jobs** without betting on either as permanently safe.
The **long runway** lets him wait for a written paid offer.

steps.text: Keep taking paid evening calls while the shift remains
Save part of evening premium toward one year of expenses
Move after 2036 only after cuts and a written offer with steady hours and mortgage-covering wages

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Nearby centres could cut their billing queues together, and a stockroom might face robots three years later. Written notice and posted paid work with enough hours and wages for our mortgage would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the evening rate disappears before any jobs formally go. A smaller pay packet can hurt a family long before a dismissal letter arrives. I would want the centre to say that out loud.

headlineQuote: A smaller pay packet can hurt a family long before a dismissal letter arrives.
portrait: Colin is a **43-year-old junior agent** with secondary schooling who still needs help on complex bills.
His **evening premium** provides higher pay, and his household holds about eight months of expenses despite a recent roof repair.
He and his **wife** support two school-age children and a mortgage; several similar centres are nearby.
He uses **AI occasionally** after proof, and checks paid shop work cautiously as robots follow thinking AI three years later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his billing wage while nearby centres shrink together.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** would make the pay risk visible before the queue changes.
A **posted paid opening** with enough hours and wages for the mortgage would permit a move.
